Hindermost
hind'er-most
a. (last; in the rear; furthest behind)
From hinder, Saxon hinder, backward, with the superlative ending. The Authorized Version uses the older form; modern printings usually read hindmost.

Biblical Definition

Two occurrences, and in each one the rearmost place tells you what somebody loved. The first is Jacob's arrangement on the morning he expected to meet Esau and possibly die: “And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost” (Gen 33:2). The order is a confession. Jacob's favourites are furthest from the danger, and Leah — the wife he never chose — stands between Rachel and the sword with her six sons. Scripture records the arrangement without a word of comment and lets the reader draw the conclusion about a house ordered by preference. The second is Babylon's sentence: “Your mother shall be sore confounded; she that bare you shall be ashamed: behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert” (Jer 50:12). The empire that had been foremost among the nations is to become the hindermost, and the land that fed the world becomes desert. The Lord states the principle that governs both texts: “So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen” (Mat 20:16).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines hindermost or hindmost as the last; that is behind all the others; and hinder as that is in a position behind another, opposed to fore.

expand to see more

HIND'ERMOST, a. superl. [from hind.] The last; that is behind all others.

HIND'MOST, a. The last; that comes or is in the rear of all others.

Rachel and Joseph hindermost. Gen. 33.

HIND'ER, a. That is in a position behind another; opposed to fore; as the hinder part of a wagon.

From Sax. hinder, backward, behind.

Key Scripture

Genesis 33:2 — "And he put the handmaids and their children foremost, and Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph hindermost."

Jeremiah 50:12 — "Your mother shall be sore confounded; she that bare you shall be ashamed: behold, the hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert."

Matthew 20:16 — "So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen."

Genesis 29:31 — "And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the order a man puts his household in reveals what he actually values.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is archaic and uncontested. What Genesis 33:2 holds is a quiet and devastating doctrine about households. Jacob had four women and eleven children, and when he thought death was coming up the road he ranked them. The handmaids and their sons went first, Leah and her six after, and Rachel and Joseph last where the danger would reach them latest. He did not announce a preference; he arranged a caravan, and the arrangement said everything. Fathers still do this, not with marching order but with attention, money, patience, and time.

The principle to recover is that God notices the hindermost and He notices the foremost, and He is not bound by either ranking. Genesis 29:31 records His response to Jacob's scale: when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb — and from that unloved wife came Judah, and from Judah came Christ. Jeremiah 50:12 shows the same reversal at the scale of empires, with the foremost of the nations becoming a desert. Matthew 20:16 states it as a law of the kingdom. Any man arranging his household by preference should reckon with the fact that the line of the Messiah ran through the wife who was placed in the middle of the column.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew acharonim (H314), the last, hindmost; acharith (H319), the latter end; Saxon hinder, backward.

expand to see more

Hebrew acharonim (H314) — the last, those behind; Genesis 33:2, of Rachel and Joseph in the rear.

Hebrew acharith goyim (H319, H1471) — the last of the nations; Jeremiah 50:12, of Babylon brought to the rear.

Hebrew senu'ah (H8130) — hated, the lesser-loved; Genesis 29:31, the Hebrew idiom for Leah's standing.

Greek hoi eschatoi protoi (G2078, G4413) — the last first; Matthew 20:16, the kingdom's reversal.

Saxon hinder — backward, behind; Webster's root, with the old superlative preserved in the Authorized Version.

Usage

"“Rachel and Joseph hindermost” — the caravan order was the confession."

"“The hindermost of the nations shall be a wilderness” — the foremost empire, brought to the rear."

"“When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb” — and Judah was born."
